clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic ANO5 variants; anoctamin-5 participates in sarcolemmal membrane repair.
One of the commoner adult-onset recessive limb-girdle dystrophies in Northern Europe, linked to the c.191dupA founder allele.
Male-predominant and often asymmetric, with prominent calf and quadriceps involvement.
May present with exercise-induced myalgia, cramps, rhabdomyolysis or asymptomatic hyperCKaemia before overt weakness.
Creatine kinase is usually markedly elevated, frequently preceding clinical weakness.
Allelic with distal Miyoshi-type myopathy (MMD3), so the phenotype spans a proximal-to-distal continuum.
The course is relatively benign with ambulation often preserved for a long period.
Cardiac involvement is uncommon but has been reported.
reference.pathophysiology: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R12 is caused by biallelic variants in ANO5 on chromosome 11p14.3, which encodes anoctamin-5, a member of the TMEM16 family that functions at the sarcolemma and its internal membranes as a phospholipid scramblase and putative calcium-activated ion channel involved in membrane repair. The recurrent c.191dupA founder variant is common in Northern European populations, making ANO5-related disease one of the more frequent adult-onset recessive limb-girdle dystrophies in that region. Defective resealing of the membrane after contraction-induced injury is thought to drive myofibre necrosis, producing a characteristically asymmetric and often male-predominant phenotype with prominent calf and quadriceps involvement, exercise-related myalgia and marked hyperCKaemia. The same gene underlies distal Miyoshi-type myopathy (MMD3) and isolated hyperCKaemia, so ANO5 disease spans a proximal-to-distal continuum.
additionalDifferentials: LGMD R2 (dysferlinopathy, with overlapping distal Miyoshi phenotype)
Miyoshi myopathy due to dysferlin (phenotypic overlap)
Metabolic and glycogen-storage myopathies presenting with rhabdomyolysis
Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy (when asymmetry raises suspicion)
additionalInvestigations: Next-generation sequencing gene panel or whole-exome sequencing including ANO5 and DYSF
Muscle MRI (asymmetric posterior thigh and calf involvement)
Muscle biopsy with dysferlin and anoctamin studies
Renal function and urinary myoglobin assessment during rhabdomyolysis episodes
redFlags: Rhabdomyolysis with dark urine and risk of acute kidney injury
Chest symptoms or breathlessness suggesting cardiomyopathy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable, with slow progression and ambulation retained for many years. Episodes of rhabdomyolysis require vigilance because of the associated risk to the kidneys.
pitfalls: Isolated hyperCKaemia may be wrongly dismissed as benign.
Phenotypic overlap with dysferlinopathy can lead to misdiagnosis without genetic testing.
Marked asymmetry may prompt inappropriate suspicion of an acquired or inflammatory cause.
Affected or carrier women may be under-recognised because of the male predominance.
references: Consensus classification of the limb-girdle muscular dystrophies
management: Recognise there is no disease-modifying drug and use physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain strength and function while avoiding overexertion that can trigger rhabdomyolysis
Recognise and treat episodes of rhabdomyolysis promptly with fluid resuscitation and renal protection
Advise on graded exercise and avoidance of muscle-injury triggers given exercise-induced myalgia and cramps
Perform baseline cardiac assessment with ECG and echocardiography and respiratory monitoring
Deliver multidisciplinary neuromuscular rehabilitation, with ambulation usually retained for many years
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and family screening
